newsitem.title: USA: Clinton wants normal China trade after HK transfer.
newsitem.headline: Clinton wants normal China trade after HK transfer.

text.p: Normal trade relations should be maintained with China despite uncertainty about the situation in Hong Kong after Beijing resumes control on July 1 and China's human rights record, U.S. President Bill Clinton said on Sunday.

"We have paid a price from time to time for our insistence on advancing human rights," he told a news conference at the end of the Denver Group of Seven summit. "I just don't think taking normal trading status away from them is much of a way to influence them over the long run."

The G7 -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- and Russia called on China in their summit communique to maintain its commitments to respect Hong Kong's freedoms when it resumes control of the British colony.
"These include ensuring Hong Kong's continued stability and prosperity and preserving its way of life, its high degree of autonomy...its fundamental freedoms and the rule of law," they said.
All but six countries enjoy so-called Most Favored Nation (MFN) trade status with the United States, which amounts to having normal trade ties.
The House of Represenetatives is scheduled to vote this week on a measure that would disapprove Clinton's decision to renew MFN for another year.
Asked if it would not be more prudent to see what happens after Hong Kong reverts to Chinese sovereignty before deciding on the trade question, Clinton said:

"If we were to basically say the United States believes we can keep you on probation all by yourself and we're going to see what you do, we're...assuming their bad faith," he added. "I think that would be a mistake."

Clinton said that under the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration China had committed itself to the "one-nation-two systems" formula, adding "that definition clearly included political as well as economic differences."
In post-summit comments, the G7 leaders differed in the tone they took on China, with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl taking the bluntest approach.

"It's very important that one makes clear to the leaders of China that the Hong Kong treaty they signed is valid. It has to be respected chapter and verse. That's a litmus test for the PRC (China), whether they like it or not," he told a news conference.

"The whole world will be watching very carefully if what was promised is kept," he added. "If China doesn't keep it, the PRC would lose its reputation as a fair solid and dependable treaty partners. If you want to say it the Asian way, they would lose face."
Other leaders took a somewhat softer tone.
"China has a long memory and we must be very strict in seeing that the 1984 agreement is applied, but also in not humiliating China," Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said.

Clinton also argued for taking a long view, saying that China had made strides on human rights since U.S. President Richard Nixon visited the country in 1972 and the United States formally recognized Beijing in 1979.

"Our frustrations with China today are not measured agaisnt the standard of 1979 and 1972," he said. "They are measured with our deep disappointment and disagreement with 1989 and Tiananmen Square," he said, referring to China's 1989 crushing of pro-democracy demonstrators in central Beijing.
